transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Doctor. Well, what brings me in is... I guess I've been eating just way too much at once. Usually it happens after my late shifts at work. I’ll stop for takeout on the way home and end up eating two burgers, a large fries, a shake... and then I still go home and clean out whatever leftovers we have in the garage fridge. It's honestly like I'm eating a whole second supper right after the first one.
When you're eating during these episodes, do you feel like you can't stop or control how much you're eating, even if you want to?

Yeah, that's exactly it. Once I start, it really feels like a switch is flipped. Even while I’m sitting there telling myself, "Roy, shut the bag and go inside," my hands just keep reaching for more. I want to stop, but I just can't seem to make myself do it.

After these episodes where you eat so much, do you do anything to try to compensate or make up for it—like making yourself vomit, using laxatives, exercising excessively, or restricting what you eat the next day?

No, I don't do anything like that. I don't throw up or take pills or anything. Sometimes I think about trying to eat less the next day, but honestly, by the time my next shift rolls around, I'm just eating my normal meals again. I don't really do anything to make up for it. I just feel bad about it and go to bed.

latest_inference.note: Ruled out F50.82 (bulimia nervosa) because patient denies compensatory behaviors (no purging, laxative use, or excessive exercise). Ruled out F50.89 (other specified feeding or eating disorder) because presentation is classic for binge eating disorder. Patient reports loss of control during eating episodes with no subsequent compensatory behaviors, which is pathognomonic for F50.81 (binge eating disorder).
